stem: This question is about Germany in 1848-50.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the revolution of 1848 in Prussia.

points.description: Street fighting in Berlin in March 1848.
Frederick William IV withdrew troops, promised a constitution / wore the national colours.
An elected Prussian assembly met.
The army returned in November 1848; the assembly was dissolved and the king imposed a constitution in December.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In March 1848 street fighting broke out in Berlin. Frederick William IV withdrew his troops, promised a constitution and appeared in the black, red and gold colours of the nationalists. An elected Prussian assembly met to draw up a constitution. But in November the army returned to Berlin, the assembly was dissolved, and in December the king imposed his own constitution.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Austria restored its influence first because it recovered from the revolutions of 1848. Its army crushed the risings in Vienna and elsewhere, and under its chief minister Schwarzenberg it regained the strength to act in Germany. Second, Austria had Russian support. When Prussia tried to form the Erfurt Union of German states under its own leadership in 1849-50, Austria demanded the restoration of the old Confederation, and Prussia, facing Austria backed by Russia, was not willing to risk war. Finally, the Erfurt Union had little real support among the German princes, so at Olmütz in November 1850 Prussia abandoned it, and the Confederation was restored in 1851 with Austria in the chair.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The king's refusal in April 1849 was decisive in one sense. The Frankfurt Parliament had chosen a Little Germany led by Prussia, and without Prussia's king and army there was no one to lead it and no force to carry out its constitution. His reasons, his belief in the divine right of kings and his fear of war with Austria, show that the princes would not accept unity offered by an elected assembly.

However, the refusal came at the end of a long decline. The parliament had no army or taxes of its own, so in 1848 it had to accept Prussia's armistice with Denmark over Schleswig-Holstein. Its members argued for months over a Greater or Little Germany, and moderate liberals feared radicals. Meanwhile the Austrian and Prussian armies had restored order by the end of 1848, and the liberals had little support among peasants and workers.

I disagree with the statement. The refusal was the final blow, but the parliament was already powerless and the old rulers had recovered; even if Frederick William had accepted, Austria, backed by Russia, would probably have prevented a united Germany, as it did at Olmütz in 1850.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the Austro-Prussian War of 1866.

points.description: Began in June 1866 after Prussian troops entered Holstein; most medium German states sided with Austria.
Italy fought on Prussia's side (Austria won at Custoza).
Moltke used railways to concentrate Prussian armies; decisive victory at Königgrätz (Sadowa), 3 July 1866.
Lasted about seven weeks; ended by the Treaty of Prague (August 1866).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The war began in June 1866 after Prussian troops entered Holstein; most of the medium-sized German states, such as Bavaria, Saxony and Hanover, sided with Austria. Italy fought on Prussia's side but was beaten by the Austrians at Custoza. Moltke used the railways to move Prussian armies quickly into Bohemia, where they defeated the main Austrian army at Königgrätz on 3 July. The war lasted about seven weeks and ended with the Treaty of Prague in August 1866.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: French opinion was already angry. France had gained nothing from Prussia's victory in 1866, had been humiliated over Luxembourg in 1867, and saw the Hohenzollern candidature for the Spanish throne as an attempt to surround it. Even after the candidature was withdrawn, the French government wanted a public guarantee. Bismarck edited King Wilhelm's report of his meeting with the French ambassador at Ems so that the king's polite refusal looked like a deliberate snub, and published it. Newspapers and crowds in Paris demanded war, and Napoleon III and his ministers feared that backing down would cost them their prestige. France declared war on 19 July 1870.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Prussia's strength was essential. Through the Zollverein it had become the economic leader of Germany, and its coal, iron and railways paid for and moved a modern army. Roon's reforms enlarged that army, the needle gun gave it superior firepower, and Moltke's planning won decisive victories at Königgrätz in 1866 and Sedan in 1870.

But strength needed to be used. Bismarck made the army reforms possible by governing without parliament's approval from 1862 to 1866. His diplomacy made sure that Prussia fought each enemy alone: Russia was won over in 1863, France stayed neutral in 1866, and Austria-Hungary and Russia stayed out in 1870. He chose the moment of each war, used Holstein and the Ems telegram to provoke conflict, made a mild peace with Austria and negotiated the southern states into the Empire.

I partly agree. Prussia's economic and military strength made unification possible, but Bismarck decided how and when that strength was used. Without him unification might have come later or in a different form; without Prussian power his diplomacy would have achieved nothing.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the Spartacist rising of January 1919.

They joined an uprising in Berlin in January 1919, aiming at a revolution like Russia's.
Ebert's government used the army and the Freikorps to crush it.
Luxemburg and Liebknecht were captured and murdered.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The Spartacists were German communists led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, who wanted a revolution like the one in Russia. In January 1919 they joined an uprising in Berlin, occupying buildings. Ebert's government called on the army and the Freikorps, which crushed the rising within days. Luxemburg and Liebknecht were captured and murdered.

Reparations led to the Ruhr occupation and hyperinflation (1923)

answerSpec.modelAnswer: The treaty weakened the republic because the new democratic politicians were blamed for it. Germans saw it as a Diktat, and nationalists called the politicians who had accepted the armistice and treaty the 'November criminals', spreading the myth that the army had been stabbed in the back. Democracy was thus linked with defeat and humiliation from the start. The military terms also angered the army and the Freikorps: the order to disband Freikorps units led directly to the Kapp Putsch of 1920. Finally, reparations caused economic crisis: when Germany fell behind with payments, France and Belgium occupied the Ruhr in 1923, and the government's response caused hyperinflation, ruining many middle-class families who blamed the republic.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
The republic recovered a great deal. The Rentenmark ended hyperinflation, and the Dawes Plan of 1924 rescheduled reparations and brought American loans, so that by 1928 industrial production was above its pre-war level. Abroad, Stresemann's Locarno Treaties of 1925, League membership in 1926 and the Kellogg-Briand Pact of 1928 made Germany a respected power again. Politically the extremes declined: the Nazis won only 2.6% of the vote in 1928.

However, the recovery had serious limits. It depended on short-term American loans that could be withdrawn, as happened after 1929. Farmers suffered from low prices and debts, and unemployment never disappeared. Coalition governments changed often, the election of Hindenburg in 1925 put a monarchist at the head of the republic, and nationalists still rejected it, as their campaign against the Young Plan in 1929 showed.

The republic recovered considerably, especially in foreign policy and the economy's surface, but the recovery was shallow, resting on foreign money and the work of one man, Stresemann, who died in October 1929.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe the methods the Nazis used to win support in 1930-33.

points.description: Propaganda organised by Goebbels: posters, rallies, films, loudspeakers, simple slogans.
Hitler's speeches; flights around Germany in the 1932 campaigns.
SA marches and violence against opponents, especially communists.
Promises tailored to different groups (work, bread, protection from communism, ending Versailles).

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Goebbels organised modern propaganda: posters, mass rallies, films, loudspeaker vans and simple slogans repeated everywhere. Hitler spoke at huge meetings and in 1932 flew from city to city to address several in one day. The SA marched through the streets and fought communists, making the Nazis look strong. The party made promises tailored to each group: work for the unemployed, protection for farmers and shopkeepers, and the destruction of the Treaty of Versailles for nationalists.

Stresemann's recovery: stable currency, prosperity and foreign success left extremists with few voters
The party was still small and reorganising; its ideas appealed to few in good times (2.6% in 1928)

answerSpec.modelAnswer: First, the Munich Putsch of 1923 failed: Hitler was imprisoned, the party was banned, and it had to be refounded in 1925 and rebuilt for the slow, legal road to power. Second, the years 1924-29 were the most prosperous of the republic. Under Stresemann the currency was stable, wages rose and Germany regained respect abroad, so few voters wanted extreme solutions. Third, the party was still small and busy reorganising, and its message of national humiliation and economic despair had little appeal in good times, so it won only 2.6% of the vote in 1928.

Other politicians played a decisive part. From 1930 Brüning governed by presidential decree under Article 48, so Germany was already ruled by a small circle around Hindenburg rather than by the Reichstag. In January 1933 it was this circle that made Hitler Chancellor: Papen, seeking revenge on Schleicher, persuaded Hindenburg to appoint Hitler with Papen as Vice-Chancellor, believing they could control him. This happened even though the Nazi vote had fallen in November 1932.

However, Hitler was only considered because of the support the Nazis had won. The Depression drove their vote from 2.6% in 1928 to 18.3% in 1930 and 37.3% in July 1932, making them the largest party. Goebbels' propaganda, the SA and Hitler's image as a strong leader persuaded millions that the Nazis could rescue Germany.

I largely agree. The Nazis' mass support made Hitler a contender, but he could not win a majority; the final decision was made by conservative politicians who misjudged him, so their actions were the most direct reason for his appointment.

parts.stem: Describe how the Enabling Act was passed in March 1933.

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: After the Reichstag Fire, an emergency decree allowed the arrest of opponents, and many communists were imprisoned. On 23 March 1933 the Reichstag met in the Kroll Opera House, surrounded by SA and SS men. The Communist deputies were absent, having been arrested or having fled, and the Catholic Centre Party voted for the Act after promises that the Church's rights would be respected. The Act passed by 444 votes to 94; only the Social Democrats voted against.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: From March 1933 Goebbels' Ministry of Propaganda controlled what Germans read and heard. Newspapers had to follow government instructions and opposition papers were closed, while cheap radios were sold so that Hitler's speeches reached most homes, with loudspeakers in streets and workplaces. Huge events such as the Nuremberg rallies and the 1936 Olympics displayed Nazi power and unity, and films carried the same message. Culture was controlled through the Reich Chamber of Culture, which artists, writers and musicians had to join; books by Jewish and anti-Nazi authors were burned in 1933, and modern art was condemned as 'degenerate'. In this way Germans heard only one point of view.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
There was opposition. Communists and socialists formed underground groups and distributed leaflets. Some church leaders resisted: Protestant pastors formed the Confessing Church, and in 1941 Bishop von Galen protested against the killing of disabled people. Some young people rejected Nazi culture, like the Edelweiss Pirates and the Swing Youth, and the White Rose students spread anti-Nazi leaflets until they were executed in 1943. In July 1944 army officers led by Stauffenberg tried to kill Hitler.

However, opposition was small, divided and rarely effective. The SS, the Gestapo and the camps made it extremely dangerous, the destruction of the other parties and the trade unions removed any way to organise, and the Gestapo received many denunciations from ordinary people. Many Germans supported the regime or accepted it because it brought jobs, order and, until 1941, foreign successes.

Overall, there was more opposition than Nazi propaganda admitted, but it involved only a small minority and never seriously threatened the regime until the bomb plot of 1944, which also failed.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: Unemployment fell partly because the government created work. Under Schacht it spent heavily on public works such as motorways and housing, and the Reich Labour Service, compulsory for young men from 1935, took them off the register. Rearmament, especially after the Four-Year Plan of 1936, created jobs in factories, and conscription from 1935 took hundreds of thousands of young men into the army. The figures were also manipulated: women pushed out of work and Jews dismissed from their jobs were not counted as unemployed, so the official fall from about six million to a few hundred thousand exaggerated the real change.

Many Germans did benefit. Millions of unemployed people found work, which after the Depression was what mattered most to them. Big businesses, especially in arms and chemicals, made large profits. Workers gained cheap holidays through Strength Through Joy and better workplaces through Beauty of Labour, farmers were protected from losing their land, and many enjoyed a sense of order and national pride.

But in 1906, just before the first Duma met, the Fundamental Laws declared that the Tsar was still the supreme autocrat: he could dissolve the Duma, make laws by decree when it was not sitting, and appoint and dismiss his ministers.

answerSpec.modelAnswer: There were deep long-term grievances. The Tsar ruled as an autocrat with no parliament; peasants were poor and wanted the landlords' land; factory workers lived and worked in harsh conditions; and national minorities resented Russification. The war with Japan from 1904 turned discontent into crisis: defeats such as the fall of Port Arthur and the destruction of the fleet at Tsushima humiliated the government, while the war raised prices and caused shortages. The spark was Bloody Sunday in January 1905, when troops fired on a peaceful procession led by Father Gapon; trust in the Tsar collapsed, and strikes, peasant risings and mutinies spread across the empire.

The revolution brought some real changes. For the first time Russia had an elected parliament, the Duma, political parties could operate openly, and censorship was relaxed. The Dumas debated and criticised ministers, and important reforms such as Stolypin's land laws followed.

**Was Bismarck responsible for the Franco-Prussian War?**

Study the sources and answer the questions that follow.

**Background information:** In July 1870 news that Prince Leopold of Hohenzollern had accepted the Spanish throne caused fury in France. The candidature was withdrawn on 12 July, but on 13 July the French ambassador asked King Wilhelm of Prussia at Ems for a promise that it would never be renewed. The king refused, and Bismarck published a shortened report of the meeting. France declared war on 19 July 1870.

**Source A** — a cartoon (described in words) of the kind published in a British satirical magazine in July 1870 (described in words; invented for this question)

> A tall figure of Bismarck in a spiked helmet stands behind a curtain, holding the strings of a small puppet dressed as a Spanish king. In front of the curtain Napoleon III, red-faced, is pulling his sword from its scabbard while a crowd behind him waves French flags. The caption reads: 'Who is pulling the strings?'

**Source B** — a letter by a fictional member of the French parliament to his wife, 16 July 1870 (invented for this question)

> The Chamber was in a fever. When the ministers read out the dispatch from Ems, men shouted that France had been slapped in the face. A few of us asked to see the full text of the report on which the government was acting. We were refused and shouted down as cowards. The vote for war credits passed amid cheering. I fear we have voted in anger for something we have not understood.

**Source C** — a report by a fictional British diplomat in Paris to the Foreign Office in London, 14 July 1870 (invented for this question)

> The withdrawal of the Prince was a victory for France, and a wise government would have been content with it. But the ministers here demanded guarantees that no king could give, and now that the Prussian report has been printed the crowds on the boulevards are crying 'To Berlin!'. I am told the Emperor himself hesitated, but those around him wanted war, and the newspapers have made retreat impossible.

**Source D** — an article in a fictional Bavarian newspaper, 20 July 1870 (invented for this question)

> France has declared war, not on Prussia alone, but on Germany. Our treaty of 1866 obliges Bavaria to stand beside Prussia; but it is not the treaty that calls us, it is our honour. The French have long wished to keep Germany divided and weak. Bavarians, whatever we have thought of Berlin, today we are Germans first.

**Source E** — an extract from the memoirs of a fictional retired Prussian staff officer, published in 1895 (invented for this question)

> In the General Staff we had been ready for war with France since 1867, and we knew our railways would carry us to the frontier first. I was present at the Foreign Ministry on the evening of 13 July when the report from Ems was shortened. Nobody in the room doubted that the new version would bring war, and nobody regretted it. The Minister-President had judged the French perfectly.

**Source F** — an editorial in a fictional French republican newspaper, 10 September 1870, after the defeat at Sedan (invented for this question)

> Let no one say that the Prussian chancellor alone brought this disaster upon France. It was the Emperor's ministers who demanded the impossible at Ems, the Emperor's newspapers that cried for war, and the Emperor's generals who swore that the army was ready to the last gaiter button. The Empire chose this war, and the Empire has lost it.

My own knowledge supports this: Bismarck had secretly encouraged Leopold's candidature, and after the meeting at Ems he shortened the king's report so that it would anger the French. The cartoon also suggests that France was walking into a trap, because Napoleon is drawing his sword in front of the curtain while the crowd cheers, unaware of who is controlling events.

Under the secret military alliance of 1866, Bavaria was obliged to support Prussia if Prussia was attacked, but many Bavarians, especially Catholics, distrusted Protestant Prussia and did not want to be ruled from Berlin. The writer's purpose was to rally Bavarians behind the war, presenting it as a war on all of Germany and appealing to honour and national feeling rather than to the treaty: 'whatever we have thought of Berlin, today we are Germans first'. It shows that, because France had declared war, Bismarck's aim of bringing the south into a national war alongside the north was succeeding.

Some sources provide evidence that Bismarck was responsible. The republic faced violence from its first weeks. In January 1919 the Spartacists, communists led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht, joined an uprising in Berlin. Ebert's government used the army and the Freikorps to crush it, and Luxemburg and Liebknecht were murdered after their capture. In the spring of 1919 further left-wing risings, including a short-lived soviet republic in Bavaria, were also put down by force.

In March 1920 the threat came from the right. Freikorps units, angry at being disbanded under the Treaty of Versailles, marched into Berlin and declared Wolfgang Kapp head of a new government. The army refused to fire on them and the government fled, but the trade unions called a general strike that stopped the city, and the putsch collapsed after four days. Soon afterwards a left-wing rising in the Ruhr was put down by the army and Freikorps.

In 1921-22 right-wing extremists carried out a wave of political murders. Matthias Erzberger, who had signed the armistice, was killed in 1921, and the foreign minister Walther Rathenau in 1922. The courts often gave right-wing killers light sentences.

The crisis year of 1923 brought more violence. During the French and Belgian occupation of the Ruhr there were clashes in which Germans were killed, and in October communists attempted a rising in Hamburg. In November Hitler and Ludendorff launched the Munich Putsch, which was stopped by Bavarian police on 9 November.

Throughout these years the republic survived, but the violence from both extremes showed how much it depended on an army and courts that did not fully support democracy.

Stresemann's importance can be judged in several ways. In the short term he saved the republic. As Chancellor in 1923 he took the unpopular decision to end passive resistance in the Ruhr and introduced the Rentenmark, which ended hyperinflation within months. Without these decisions the republic might have collapsed in 1923.

He was also important for the economy. As foreign minister he negotiated the Dawes Plan of 1924, which rescheduled reparations and brought large American loans, and the Young Plan of 1929, which reduced the total. American money paid for new factories, housing and public works, and by 1928 production was above its pre-war level.

His greatest achievements were in foreign policy. At Locarno in 1925 Germany accepted its western borders and was treated as an equal; in 1926 it joined the League of Nations with a permanent seat on the Council; and in 1928 it signed the Kellogg-Briand Pact. His policy of co-operation won the early evacuation of the Ruhr and, later, of the Rhineland. He shared the Nobel Peace Prize in 1926.

Politically, this success helped to stabilise the republic. Extremist parties declined: the Nazis won only 2.6% of the vote in 1928. Stresemann, a respected figure in every government from 1923 to 1929, helped to hold coalitions together.

However, his importance has limits. The recovery rested mainly on American loans, which he did not control, and on the work of others, such as Schacht at the central bank and the Dawes committee. Serious weaknesses remained: farmers suffered, coalitions were unstable, and in 1925 the monarchist Hindenburg was elected President. In the long term, his achievements did not survive the Depression, and he died in October 1929, just before the Wall Street Crash.

Overall Stresemann was the most important individual in the republic's survival and recovery. He saved it in 1923 and made it respected abroad, but the recovery he led was fragile because it depended on forces beyond his control, so his importance was great in the short term and limited in the long term.

After the Wall Street Crash of October 1929, American loans were withdrawn and unemployment rose rapidly in Germany. In March 1930 the coalition government collapsed over the cost of unemployment benefits, and the new Chancellor, Heinrich Brüning, governed by presidential decree under Article 48.

In the election of September 1930 the Nazis jumped from 12 to 107 seats, winning 18.3% of the vote. Goebbels' propaganda, mass rallies and the marching SA presented the party as the energetic answer to the crisis, and it won support from farmers, the middle classes and many young people.

In the spring of 1932 Hitler stood for President against Hindenburg. He lost, but he won about 37% of the vote in the second round. In June Hindenburg replaced Brüning with Franz von Papen, who had little support in the Reichstag. In the election of July 1932 the Nazis won 37.3% and 230 seats, becoming the largest party, but Hindenburg refused to make Hitler Chancellor.

In November 1932 another election saw the Nazi vote fall to 33.1%. In December General Kurt von Schleicher replaced Papen but also failed to build a majority. Papen, seeking revenge, met Hitler in January 1933 and agreed to serve under him, and he persuaded Hindenburg that the conservatives could control Hitler, since there would be only three Nazis in the cabinet.

On 30 January 1933 Hindenburg appointed Hitler Chancellor, with Papen as Vice-Chancellor.

The importance of the Night of the Long Knives can be judged by what it achieved, by comparison with other steps, and by its long-term effects.

It removed the greatest remaining threat to Hitler. The SA, with millions of members, was led by Ernst Röhm, who wanted a 'second revolution' and to merge the SA with the army. On 30 June 1934 SS units killed Röhm and other SA leaders, and Hitler used the purge to murder old enemies such as Schleicher and Strasser. No one inside the Nazi movement could challenge him afterwards.

It also won over the army. The generals, who had feared the SA, were relieved, and when Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934 they accepted Hitler as Führer, and every soldier swore an oath of personal loyalty to him. This tied the one institution that could have removed Hitler to his person.

It showed, too, that Hitler would kill his opponents and that the law would approve it afterwards, which spread fear, and it raised the SS, which soon controlled the police and the camps.

However, the foundations of the dictatorship had been laid earlier. The emergency decree after the Reichstag Fire in February 1933 suspended civil rights, and the Enabling Act of March 1933 gave Hitler the power to make laws without the Reichstag. Using it, the Nazis abolished the trade unions, banned the other parties and took over the state governments. By July 1933 Germany was a one-party state. Hindenburg's death and the plebiscite of August 1934 were also needed before Hitler became Führer.

Overall the Night of the Long Knives was the step that completed the dictatorship rather than the one that created it. The Enabling Act gave Hitler legal power, but the purge removed the last rivals inside his movement and won the army's loyalty, so it was essential to the dictatorship's security.

Persecution began soon after the Nazis took power. On 1 April 1933 the SA organised a boycott of Jewish shops, standing outside them to turn customers away. In the same month Jews were dismissed from the civil service, including teaching, and in the following years they were excluded from many other professions and from the arts. Nazi newspapers and the school curriculum spread anti-Semitic ideas.

In September 1935 the Nuremberg Laws took away Jews' German citizenship and banned marriages and relationships between Jews and non-Jewish Germans. Persecution eased slightly during the 1936 Olympics, when foreign visitors were in Germany, but in 1938 it became much harsher: Jews had to register their property, and Jewish businesses were increasingly taken over by non-Jews.

On 9-10 November 1938, after a German diplomat was shot in Paris by a young Jewish refugee, the Nazis organised Kristallnacht. Across Germany and Austria Jewish homes and shops were attacked and hundreds of synagogues burned; historians estimate that about 90 Jews were killed and about 30,000 Jewish men sent to concentration camps. Afterwards the Jewish community was fined one billion Reichsmarks, Jewish children were expelled from German schools, and Jews were driven out of economic life.

Many Jews tried to emigrate, and about half of Germany's Jews had left by 1939, although they had to leave most of their property behind and many countries limited the number of refugees they accepted. By the outbreak of war, those who remained had lost their rights, their livelihoods and their safety.

Propaganda was very important. From March 1933 Goebbels' Ministry of Propaganda controlled the press, radio and films, so Germans heard only the regime's view. Cheap radios brought Hitler's speeches into most homes, and loudspeakers carried them into streets and workplaces.

Propaganda also created enthusiasm. The Nuremberg rallies and the 1936 Olympics displayed power and unity, and the cult of Hitler presented him as the saviour of Germany. Through schools, the Hitler Youth and the Reich Chamber of Culture, Nazi ideas reached the young and shaped what people read, watched and heard. Propaganda prepared Germans to accept the persecution of Jews and other groups by presenting them as enemies.

However, propaganda was not the only method. Terror was just as important: the SS and the Gestapo arrested opponents without trial, the camps held communists, socialists and others, and the courts were controlled. The destruction of other parties and the trade unions in 1933 meant there was no organised way to oppose the regime.

The regime also won real support through its achievements. Unemployment fell from about six million to a few hundred thousand, order returned to the streets, and Hitler's foreign successes before 1939 made him popular. Propaganda worked best when it could point to real gains. It also had limits: some young people rejected the Hitler Youth, the churches kept some independence, and as the war turned against Germany after 1942 propaganda convinced fewer people.

Overall propaganda was important because it shaped how Germans saw the regime and made terror seem justified, but it worked together with terror and with genuine popular support. On its own it could not have kept the Nazis in power; without it, terror alone would have been far less effective.

By January 1905 Russia was losing the war with Japan: Port Arthur had just fallen, and prices and shortages were causing hardship in the cities. On 22 January (9 January, old style) Father Gapon led a peaceful procession of workers to the Winter Palace in St Petersburg to petition the Tsar. Troops opened fire, killing many; the day became known as Bloody Sunday.

In the following months strikes spread through the cities, peasants attacked landlords' estates, and there were risings in Poland and other national borderlands. In May the Russian fleet was destroyed at Tsushima, and in June the sailors of the battleship Potemkin mutinied in the Black Sea.

In September the Treaty of Portsmouth ended the war with Japan. In October a general strike paralysed the country, and workers in St Petersburg formed a soviet, in which Leon Trotsky played a leading part. On 30 October (17 October) the Tsar, on Witte's advice, issued the October Manifesto, promising civil rights and an elected Duma. Most liberals accepted it, and the opposition split.

With peace made and most of the army still loyal, the government struck back. In December the leaders of the St Petersburg Soviet were arrested and an armed rising in Moscow was crushed with artillery. By early 1906 the Tsar had regained control, and redemption payments were reduced to calm the peasants.

Rasputin's importance can be judged by his effect on the monarchy's reputation, on government, and in comparison with other causes.

Rasputin, a Siberian holy man, gained influence at court because he seemed able to help the Tsar's son Alexei, who had haemophilia. Stories about his drinking and behaviour, and about his power over the Tsarina, spread widely and damaged the royal family's prestige among nobles, Duma members and ordinary people alike.

His influence grew after September 1915, when Nicholas took command of the army and left the Tsarina, Alexandra, in charge in Petrograd. Rasputin was believed to influence the appointment and dismissal of ministers, which were changed so often that government became chaotic just when Russia needed efficient leadership in the war. Because the Tsarina was German-born, rumours spread that the court was influenced by Germany, weakening loyalty even among the Tsar's natural supporters. In December 1916 a group of nobles murdered Rasputin, a sign of how far the elite had turned against the court.

However, other factors were more important. The First World War brought defeat, millions of casualties, food and fuel shortages and inflation, and after 1915 the Tsar was personally blamed for military failure. Long-term weaknesses, autocracy, peasant land hunger, poor conditions for workers and the broken promises of 1905, meant that the regime had little support to fall back on. The decisive moment came in March 1917, when the soldiers of the Petrograd garrison refused to fire on the crowds.

Overall Rasputin was more a symptom of the regime's weakness than a cause of its collapse. He mattered because he destroyed the respect on which the monarchy depended and contributed to chaotic government during the war, but the regime would have been in serious danger without him; the war and the loss of the army's loyalty were far more important.

Opposition to Bolshevik rule grew after the closure of the Constituent Assembly in January 1918 and the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March, which gave up huge territories to Germany. In May 1918 the Czech Legion, former prisoners of war travelling east, rebelled and seized much of the Trans-Siberian Railway, and anti-Bolshevik governments formed behind them. Britain, France, the USA, Japan and other countries landed troops in the north, south and east.

In July 1918, as Czech and White forces approached Yekaterinburg, the Bolsheviks shot Nicholas II and his family. After an attempt on Lenin's life in August, the Cheka began the Red Terror against suspected opponents. Meanwhile Trotsky, as Commissar for War, built the Red Army by conscription, using former Tsarist officers watched by commissars, and War Communism seized grain and controlled industry to supply it.

In 1919 the Whites launched their main offensives. Admiral Kolchak advanced from Siberia in the spring, General Denikin from the south in the summer, reaching Orel, south of Moscow, and General Yudenich towards Petrograd in the autumn. Because the Whites attacked separately, the Reds defeated them one by one; Trotsky took charge of the defence of Petrograd.

In 1920 the Bolsheviks fought a war with Poland, and the last White army, under Wrangel, was evacuated from Crimea in November 1920. By 1921 the Reds had won, but War Communism had caused famine and peasant revolts, and in March 1921 the Kronstadt sailors rebelled, leading Lenin to introduce the New Economic Policy.

Lenin's importance can be judged by the decisions he took that others would not have taken, and by comparing his role with other factors.

In 1917 his role was decisive. When he returned in April, many Bolsheviks were willing to co-operate with the Provisional Government, but his April Theses demanded opposition to it, an end to the war and all power to the soviets. 'Peace, Land and Bread' matched what millions wanted. In October he persuaded a reluctant Central Committee to vote for an armed rising.

In power he acted quickly and ruthlessly. The Decrees on Peace and Land won support; the Cheka was founded; and when the Constituent Assembly refused to accept Bolshevik rule, he closed it. Against strong opposition in his own party he insisted on accepting the Treaty of Brest-Litovsk, arguing that peace was the price of survival.

During the Civil War Lenin led the government, introduced War Communism and backed the Red Terror, keeping the party united and the army supplied. In 1921, after the Kronstadt Rising, he showed flexibility by introducing the NEP, while the ban on factions tightened the party's control.

However, others were also vital. Trotsky organised the seizure of power through the Military Revolutionary Committee and built the Red Army that won the Civil War. The Bolsheviks were helped by the failures of the Provisional Government, especially the war and the Kornilov affair, by their central position in Russia and by the divisions of the Whites.

Overall Lenin was the most important single factor. Others carried out his decisions, and circumstances favoured the Bolsheviks, but without his insistence on seizing power in 1917, accepting peace in 1918 and retreating to the NEP in 1921, the Bolsheviks would probably not have gained power or kept it.

In 1928 Stalin abandoned the NEP and launched the first Five-Year Plan. Gosplan, the state planning agency, set targets for every industry, mine and factory, concentrating on heavy industry: coal, iron and steel, oil, electricity and machinery. The targets were very high and were often raised, and the first plan was declared complete in four years, in 1932.

Huge projects were built. The new steel city of Magnitogorsk rose in the Urals, the Dnieper dam was completed in 1932, and the White Sea Canal was dug by Gulag prisoners and opened in 1933. Workers were driven by piece rates, bonuses and propaganda, and by harsh discipline; from 1932 internal passports restricted their movement.

The second plan (1933-37) continued to build heavy industry but gave more attention to transport and some consumer goods; the Moscow Metro opened in 1935. In 1935 the miner Alexei Stakhanov was reported to have cut many times his quota of coal in one shift, and the Stakhanovite movement encouraged workers to beat their targets.

The third plan, from 1938, turned increasingly to armaments as war approached, and it was interrupted by the German invasion in June 1941.

By 1941 production of coal, steel and electricity had grown many times over, and much industry had been built in the east, beyond the reach of invaders. But the plans also brought poor quality, waste, false figures, shortages of consumer goods and great human suffering.

Terror was central to Stalin's control, but its importance should be weighed against other methods.

First, terror removed every possible rival. After Kirov's murder in 1934, the show trials of 1936-38 destroyed the Old Bolsheviks: Zinoviev and Kamenev were shot in 1936 and Bukharin in 1938. In 1937 Marshal Tukhachevsky and many senior officers were executed, so the army could not challenge Stalin either.

Second, terror created fear throughout society. In the Great Terror of 1937-38, historians estimate from Soviet archives that about 1.5 million people were arrested and about 680,000 executed. The NKVD arrested people at night, and millions passed through the Gulag. Fear meant that people denounced others to protect themselves and that no one dared to organise opposition.

Third, terror enforced economic policy. Peasants who resisted collectivisation were labelled kulaks and deported, managers who failed were accused of being 'wreckers', and harsh laws punished workers for lateness or absence.

However, other factors also mattered. As General Secretary, Stalin controlled appointments, and the purges themselves created a new generation of officials who owed everything to him. Propaganda and the cult of personality presented him as the wise father of the peoples, and socialist realism and education shaped what people believed. The regime also had real achievements: jobs, education and promotion for millions of workers and peasants' children, which won genuine support from some.

Overall terror was the most important method of control by 1941, because it destroyed every alternative source of power and made opposition unthinkable. But it worked together with propaganda and the party machine; terror alone created chaos and weakened the economy and the army, while propaganda and opportunity won the loyalty that fear could not.
